title: Boundary homeomorphism carrying a simplex horn to a cylinder bottom
statement: For $n\geq2$ and $0\leq i\leq n$, identify the realization of the standard $n$-simplex with $\Delta^n=\{(t_0,\ldots,t_n)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:t_j\geq0,\sum_jt_j=1\}$. Let $H_i=\{t\in\Delta^n:\text{ some }t_j=0\text{ with }j\ne i\}$ be the realized $i$-th horn, let $F_i=\{t\in\Delta^n:t_i=0\}$ be the opposite face, and let $\partial\Delta^n$ and $\partial(F_i\times[0,1])$ denote the frontiers relative to their affine spans; all spaces and subsets have their Euclidean subspace topologies [def-kun-subspace-topology]. There is a homeomorphism $\psi:\partial\Delta^n\to\partial(F_i\times[0,1])$ whose restriction maps $H_i$ homeomorphically onto $F_i\times\{0\}$.

source.place: Boundary/horn paragraph after Proposition 3.2.2 and before Proposition 3.2.3, printed p.79; explicit coning and radial-coordinate construction.

proof.text: Write $F=F_i$, $H=H_i$, $J=\{0,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i\}$, and $c_i=0$, $c_j=1/n$ for $j\in J$. For $x\in F$ put $m(x)=\min_{j\in J}x_j$ and $r(x)=1-nm(x)$. Since $|J|=n$ and $\sum_{j\in J}x_j=1$, we have $0\leq m\leq1/n$, $0\leq r\leq1$, and $r=0$ exactly at $c$. Finite minima are continuous: iterate $\min(a,b)=(a+b-|a-b|)/2$. The relative interior of $F$ consists precisely of points with all $x_j>0$ for $j\in J$: strict inequalities persist on a small relative ball; if $x_j=0$, decreasing this coordinate and increasing another $J$-coordinate stays in the affine span but exits $F$. Thus $B=\partial F=\{x\in F:m(x)=0\}$. The same argument with all $n+1$ coordinates gives $\partial\Delta^n=H\cup F$ and $H\cap F=B$. Applying the strict-inequality argument also to $0\leq s\leq1$ gives $\partial(F\times[0,1])=(F\times\{0\})\cup S$, where $S=(B\times[0,1])\cup(F\times\{1\})$. These are finite unions of coordinate-zero or endpoint sets, hence closed in the indicated subspaces. Here and below the subspace topology is [def-kun-subspace-topology].

source.place: Agent expansion of Hovey, Model Categories, paragraph after Proposition 3.2.2, printed p.79 (PDF index 88); explicit barycentric formulas supplying the omitted boundary-pair argument.

proof.text: Define $\alpha:H\to F$ by $\alpha(t)_i=0$ and $\alpha(t)_j=t_j+t_i/n$ for $j\in J$. Its coordinates are nonnegative and sum to $1$. Because some $t_j=0$ with $j\in J$, $m(\alpha(t))=t_i/n$. Conversely define $a:F\to H$ by $a(x)_i=nm(x)$ and $a(x)_j=x_j-m(x)$ for $j\in J$. These coordinates are nonnegative, sum to $1$, and one $J$-coordinate is zero. Substitution gives $a\alpha(t)=t$ and $\alpha a(x)=x$. Both maps are continuous by their coordinate formulas and continuity of $m$ from step 1. They restrict to the identity on $B$, where $m=0$ and $t_i=0$. Thus $\alpha$ is a homeomorphism fixing $B$.

source.place: Agent expansion of Hovey, Model Categories, paragraph after Proposition 3.2.2, printed p.79 (PDF index 88); explicit barycentric formulas supplying the omitted boundary-pair argument.

proof.text:
Define $\beta:F\to S$ on the closed cover $F_{\leq}=\{r\leq1/2\}$, $F_{\geq}=\{r\geq1/2\}$ by
$$\beta(x)=\begin{cases}(c+2(x-c),1),&r(x)\leq1/2,\\(c+(x-c)/r(x),2-2r(x)),&r(x)\geq1/2.\end{cases}$$
The first spatial coordinate has sum $1$ and minimum $2m(x)-1/n\geq0$, so lies in $F$. In the second branch put $u=c+(x-c)/r(x)$; for $j\in J$, $u_j=(x_j-m(x))/r(x)\geq0$, its sum is $1$, and one coordinate is zero, so $u\in B$. Also $2-2r\in[0,1]$. At $r=1/2$ both formulas give $(c+2(x-c),1)$; at $r=0$ the first gives $(c,1)$, and at $r=1$ the second gives $(x,0)$. The first branch is affine and the second has a denominator bounded below by $1/2$, so both are continuous on their closed domains. Apply [lem-coef-closed-union-continuity] on $X=F$ to the resulting well-defined function (with codomain the ambient Euclidean product), then use its image in $S$ with the induced topology [def-kun-subspace-topology]. This proves continuity of $\beta$.

source.place: Agent expansion of Hovey, Model Categories, paragraph after Proposition 3.2.2, printed p.79 (PDF index 88); explicit barycentric formulas supplying the omitted boundary-pair argument.

proof.text: Define $b:S\to F$ on the top and side by $b(y,1)=(c+y)/2$ for $y\in F$, and $b(u,s)=c+(1-s/2)(u-c)$ for $u\in B$, $s\in[0,1]$. These points lie in $F$ by coordinate nonnegativity and sum $1$. On the intersection $B\times\{1\}$ the two formulas agree. The top and side are closed in $S$ by step 1 and each formula is continuous, so [lem-coef-closed-union-continuity] proves continuity of $b$. For $y\in F$, $m((c+y)/2)=1/(2n)+m(y)/2$, hence $r((c+y)/2)=r(y)/2\leq1/2$; substitution into the first branch of $\beta$ returns $(y,1)$. For $u\in B$, $m(b(u,s))=s/(2n)$ and $r(b(u,s))=1-s/2\geq1/2$; substitution into the second branch returns $(u,s)$. Conversely, on the first branch $b\beta(x)=(c+c+2(x-c))/2=x$, and on the second it is $c+r(x)((x-c)/r(x))=x$. Thus $b$ and $\beta$ are continuous inverses, and $\beta(u)=(u,0)$ for $u\in B$.

source.place: Agent expansion of Hovey, Model Categories, paragraph after Proposition 3.2.2, printed p.79 (PDF index 88); explicit barycentric formulas supplying the omitted boundary-pair argument.

proof.text: On $\partial\Delta^n=H\cup F$ set $\psi(t)=(\alpha(t),0)$ on $H$ and $\psi(x)=\beta(x)$ on $F$. On their intersection $B$, both formulas give $(u,0)$ by steps 2 and 3. They therefore define a function, continuous on each of the two closed pieces and hence continuous by [lem-coef-closed-union-continuity]. Its inverse on $\partial(F\times[0,1])=(F\times\{0\})\cup S$ is $(x,0)\mapsto a(x)$ on the bottom and $(y,s)\mapsto b(y,s)$ on $S$. On the intersection $B\times\{0\}$ both give $u$: $a(u)=u$ and $b(u,0)=u$. The bottom and $S$ are closed, and these inverse formulas are continuous, so the same cited lemma proves continuity of the inverse. All restrictions and maps into these subspaces use [def-kun-subspace-topology]. The inverse identities follow from $a\alpha=1$, $\alpha a=1$, $b\beta=1$, and $\beta b=1$ already checked. Finally $\psi|_H=(\alpha,0)$ is a homeomorphism onto $F\times\{0\}$, since $\alpha:H\to F$ is a homeomorphism. This is the asserted boundary homeomorphism with its required horn restriction.
